planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery starts in fall so roots establish before winter rains, setting the crown slightly proud of the soil surface to prevent rot.

directions: Plant on a rocky slope, rock wall, or raised bed with sharp drainage, tucking the base into gravel or crevices so winter rain sheds away from the crown. Water sparingly during the growing season and keep completely dry through the summer dormancy that follows its spring bloom. The thick, chalky-white leaves form a striking rosette that reflects heat and rarely needs supplemental water once established. Its coral-pink flower stalks rise above the foliage in late spring, drawing hummingbirds to coastal and inland rock gardens.

common_name: Jellybean Plant (Pork and Beans, Sedum rubrotinctum)

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in dry, gritty mix after the last frost, letting cut ends callus for a few days before setting them in soil.

directions: Grow in shallow containers or as a groundcover in fast-draining succulent mix, watering only when the soil is fully dry and allowing bright sun to bring out the plant's best color. Individual leaves detach easily and root readily where they fall, so it spreads quickly along rock edges and container rims. Its plump, bean-shaped leaves turn from jade green to ruby red under strong light and cool temperatures, giving the plant its jellybean nickname. Small star-shaped yellow flowers appear on short stalks in spring above the trailing foliage.

planting.note: Take stem cuttings in spring, callus the cut ends for two to three days, then set into gritty succulent mix and water lightly until roots form.

directions: Plant in well-drained containers or rock gardens with full sun exposure to develop its signature copper-orange coloring, which fades to yellow-green in shade. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings and protect the plant from frost, bringing containers indoors where winters are cold. The fleshy, pointed leaves form loose rosettes on trailing stems that cascade attractively over pot edges and low walls. Clusters of small white star-shaped flowers appear on tall stalks above the foliage in late winter or spring.

common_name: String of Buttons (Necklace Vine, Crassula perforata)

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings after the cut end has callused for a few days, then insert into gritty succulent mix and keep barely moist until roots take hold.

directions: Grow in hanging baskets or shallow pots with fast-draining succulent mix, providing bright but filtered light to avoid scorching the pale foliage. Let the soil dry out fully between waterings and reduce water further in winter. Triangular gray-green leaves are stacked in opposite pairs along trailing stems, threading through each other in a way that gives the plant its common name. In warm weather mature plants send up small clusters of star-shaped white or pale pink flowers at the stem tips.

planting.note: Set rooted offsets into gritty, fast-draining soil in spring, spacing rosettes far enough apart that mature leaves will not overlap.

directions: Plant in shallow, wide containers or rock garden pockets with gritty succulent mix, giving full sun to keep the rosette compact and densely covered in fine white hairs. Water deeply but infrequently, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent rot in the fuzzy foliage. The tight rosette of spoon-shaped leaves is coated in soft bristles that give it a frosted, silvery appearance year-round. In late winter to spring, arching stalks rise from the rosette bearing bell-shaped red-and-yellow flowers reminiscent of small firecrackers.

common_name: Lace Aloe (Guinea Fowl Aloe, Aristaloe aristata)

planting.note: Divide and replant offset rosettes in spring into gritty, well-drained soil, setting the base at the same depth it grew previously.

directions: Grow in containers or rock gardens with sharply drained soil and light afternoon shade in hot climates, watering only when the soil has dried out completely. It tolerates brief light frosts better than many aloes, making it useful in border zones between hardy and tender succulent plantings. The stemless rosette of dark green, white-spotted leaves edged in soft translucent teeth resembles a small starfish and slowly offsets into a dense clump. Coral-orange tubular flowers appear on slender stalks above the foliage in spring.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts in spring on a raised, gritty scree slope that drains rapidly and never sits in standing water.

directions: Site on a steep, well-drained slope or raised bed of gritty, mineral-rich soil that mimics its native mountain habitat, and avoid summer overhead watering that can rot the tightly packed leaves. This alpine aloe tolerates cold and occasional snow better than most aloes but demands excellent drainage year-round. Mature rosettes form a striking five-pointed spiral of thick, blue-green leaves that can spiral clockwise or counterclockwise. Established plants send up dense spikes of red-orange tubular flowers in late spring, though it may take several years to bloom from a young offset.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown starts in spring in a raised bed or slope of coarse, mineral gravel with no organic mulch against the crown.

directions: Plant in full sun on a rocky slope or berm with fast-draining, gravelly soil, keeping the crown high and dry to survive freezing winters. This is among the cold-hardiest agaves, tolerating temperatures well below freezing as long as its roots stay dry. The compact, symmetrical rosette of narrow, blue-gray leaves is armed with small marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine, forming clumps over time through basal offsets. Like other agaves it is monocarpic, sending up a tall flower spike once after many years before that individual rosette dies.

common_name: Soapweed Yucca (Small Soapweed, Great Plains Yucca)

planting.note: Set root divisions or nursery transplants in spring into a sunny, well-drained bed and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established.

directions: Plant in full sun on dry, sandy or rocky ground and skip supplemental irrigation once roots are established, since this prairie native thrives on neglect. It is one of the most cold- and drought-tolerant yuccas, surviving harsh Great Plains winters and prolonged summer drought without protection. Narrow, rigid, blue-green leaves with curling white fibers along the margins form low clumping rosettes that stay evergreen year-round. In early summer a stout central stalk rises with a cluster of large, waxy, greenish-white bell-shaped flowers favored by native pollinators.

planting.note: Let a removed pad callus for one to two weeks in a dry spot, then set it upright an inch deep in gritty, mineral soil after the danger of hard frost has passed.

directions: Plant rooted pads in full sun in sharply drained, gravelly soil and withhold water almost entirely once established, since this desert native rots quickly in damp conditions. It spreads slowly into low, sprawling mats and tolerates both intense heat and winter cold in dry desert and high-plateau gardens. The flattened, blue-gray to purplish pads are covered in dense tufts of tiny golden glochids rather than long spines, giving them a smooth, beaver-tail-like appearance that belies their irritating prickle. Vivid magenta-pink flowers appear along the pad edges in spring, followed by dry, spiny fruit.

common_name: Pig's Ear Plant (Round-Leaf Navelwort, Cotyledon orbiculata)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing for several days, then plant into gritty, well-drained soil in a full-sun bed or container once frost danger has passed.

directions: Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil, watering deeply but infrequently and allowing the soil to dry between waterings to keep the fleshy stems from rotting. It forms a small, woody-based shrub over time, tolerating coastal wind and salt spray as well as drought. Thick, chalky gray-green paddle-shaped leaves often develop a reddish, crinkled margin in strong sun, giving the plant its pig's-ear common name. Clusters of dangling, tubular orange to red flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage in summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators.
